claim: Learning to be safe is central for adaptive behaviour when threats are no longer present.
source: Learning to be safe is central for adaptive behaviour when threats are no longer present.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of safety learning, drawing from established scientific understanding.

claim: Detecting the absence of an expected threat is key for threat extinction learning and an essential process for the behavioural treatment of anxiety-related disorders.
source: Detecting the absence of an expected threat is key for threat extinction learning and an essential process for the behavioural treatment of anxiety-related disorders.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about extinction learning mechanisms and their clinical relevance.

claim: Dopaminergic enhancement via administration of L-DOPA (vs. Placebo) was associated with reduced retention of differential psychophysiological threat responses at later test.
source: Dopaminergic enhancement via administration of L-DOPA (vs. Placebo) was associated with reduced retention of differential psychophysiological threat responses at later test, which was mediated by activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex that was specific to extinction learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study comparing L-DOPA and Placebo groups.

claim: The effect of L-DOPA on reduced retention of differential psychophysiological threat responses was mediated by activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex that was specific to extinction learning.
source: Dopaminergic enhancement via administration of L-DOPA (vs. Placebo) was associated with reduced retention of differential psychophysiological threat responses at later test, which was mediated by activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex that was specific to extinction learning.
evidence: This mediation relationship is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: L-DOPA administration enhanced signals at the time-point of an expected, but omitted threat in extinction learning within the nucleus accumbens.
source: L-DOPA administration enhanced signals at the time-point of an expected, but omitted threat in extinction learning within the nucleus accumbens, which were functionally coupled with the ventral tegmental area and the amygdala.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data showing enhanced nucleus accumbens activity in the L-DOPA group.

claim: Nucleus accumbens signals at the time-point of omitted threat were functionally coupled with the ventral tegmental area and the amygdala.
source: L-DOPA administration enhanced signals at the time-point of an expected, but omitted threat in extinction learning within the nucleus accumbens, which were functionally coupled with the ventral tegmental area and the amygdala.
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analysis from fMRI data.

claim: Computational modelling of threat expectancies revealed prediction error encoding in nucleus accumbens that was reduced when L-DOPA was administered.
source: Computational modelling of threat expectancies further revealed prediction error encoding in nucleus accumbens that was reduced when L-DOPA was administered.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Extinction learning is influenced by L-DOPA.
source: Our results thereby provide evidence that extinction learning is influenced by L-DOPA and provide a mechanistic perspective to augment extinction learning by dopaminergic enhancement in humans.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Safety learning deficits characterise symptoms in a wide range of anxiety-related disorders.
source: As such, safety learning is central for adaptive behaviour and deficits characterise symptoms in a wide range of anxiety-related disorders (Duits et al., 2015; Fenster et al., 2018; Lissek et al., 2005; Milad and Quirk, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The neuropharmacological mechanism to augment safety learning by encoding the absence of potential threats or aversive outcomes in humans are not completely understood.
source: Yet, the neuropharmacological mechanism to augment safety learning by encoding the absence of potential threats or aversive outcomes in humans are not completely understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Extinction learning involves learning of a new CS–no US association that inhibits the acquired CS–US association.
source: Extinction learning is held to involve learning of a new CS–no US association that inhibits the acquired CS–US association (Bouton, 2004; Bouton and Nelson, 1994).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Studies in Drosophila and rodents revealed that the omission of an expected aversive outcomes depends on signals in the dopaminergic system.
source: Studies in Drosophila (Felsenberg et al., 2018) and rodents (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Correia et al., 2016; Holtzman-Assif et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2018; Mueller et al., 2010; Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020; Aksoy-Aksel et al., 2021) revealed that the omission of an expected aversive outcomes depends on signals in the dopaminergic system.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to animal studies.

claim: In rodents, processing of omitted aversive outcomes involved dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), the nucleus accumbens, and the medial prefrontal cortex, as well as projections between the VTA and nucleus accumbens.
source: In rodents, this involved dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), the nucleus accumbens, and the medial prefrontal cortex, as well as projections between the VTA and nucleus accumbens (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2018; Oleson et al., 2012; Rodriguez-Romaguera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent studies.

claim: The VTA, nucleus accumbens, and vmPFC were found to underpin the processing of rewarding outcomes.
source: Importantly, these neural regions were also found to underpin the processing of rewarding outcomes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about reward processing in the brain.

claim: When signalling rewards, the dopaminergic system codes a difference between the expected reward and the actual outcome in form of an expectancy violation or prediction error.
source: When signalling rewards, this system does not simply detect a rewarding outcome, but codes a difference between the expected reward and the actual outcome in form of an expectancy violation or prediction error (Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a seminal study on reward prediction errors.

claim: Reward-related response in the VTA, nucleus accumbens, and vmPFC reflect outcomes that are better than expected.
source: In other words, reward-related response in the VTA, nucleus accumbens, and vmPFC reflect outcomes that are better than expected.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established knowledge about reward prediction error signaling.

claim: The omission of an expected aversive US might be under the influence of a dopaminergic signal that encodes an expectancy violation.
source: Similarly, the omission of an expected aversive US, which could be framed as 'better than expected', might well be under the influence of a dopaminergic signal: At the time-point of US omission, a dopaminergic system might encode an expectancy violation that signals the difference between the expected aversive US and the omitted aversive outcome (for review, see Abraham et al., 2014; Kalisch et al., 2019; Nasser and McNally, 2012; Sartori and Singewald, 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by review citations and theoretical reasoning.

claim: Two functional neuroimaging studies in humans provided initial evidence that computational modelling of a prediction error for the omitted aversive outcome during extinction training involves activity in the nucleus accumbens.
source: Even though this idea has not been formally tested, it is supported by two functional neuroimaging study in humans. These studies provided initial evidence that computational modelling of an prediction error for the omitted aversive outcome during extinction training involves activity in the nucleus accumbens (Thiele et al., 2021; Raczka et al., 2011) and that this activity was modulated by a genetic variance of the dopamine transporter gene (Raczka et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two neuroimaging studies.

claim: Nucleus accumbens activity during extinction training was modulated by a genetic variance of the dopamine transporter gene.
source: These studies provided initial evidence that computational modelling of an prediction error for the omitted aversive outcome during extinction training involves activity in the nucleus accumbens (Thiele et al., 2021; Raczka et al., 2011) and that this activity was modulated by a genetic variance of the dopamine transporter gene (Raczka et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: There is cross-species evidence for enhanced extinction memory consolidation by augmented dopaminergic transmission after extinction training by administration of L-DOPA.
source: Additionally, there is cross-species evidence for enhanced extinction memory consolidation by augmented dopaminergic transmission after extinction training (by administration of L-DOPA [Gerlicher et al., 2018; Haaker et al., 2015; Haaker et al., 2013]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Dopaminergic enhancement of extinction memory retrieval is mediated by augmenting activity in the ventral part of the medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC).
source: These latter studies suggest that dopaminergic enhancement of extinction memory retrieval is mediated by augmenting activity in the ventral part of the medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), a structure that is central for extinction learning and memory retrieval (Kalisch et al., 2006; Milad et al., 2007; Milad and Quirk, 2002; Phelps et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The vmPFC is a structure that is central for extinction learning and memory retrieval.
source: These latter studies suggest that dopaminergic enhancement of extinction memory retrieval is mediated by augmenting activity in the ventral part of the medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), a structure that is central for extinction learning and memory retrieval (Kalisch et al., 2006; Milad et al., 2007; Milad and Quirk, 2002; Phelps et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: It is not clear if enhancing of dopaminergic neurotransmission would strengthen extinction learning by modulating vmPFC activity.
source: It is, however, not clear if enhancing of dopaminergic neurotransmission would strengthen extinction learning by modulating vmPFC activity.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Participants in both groups learned CS–US contingencies during acquisition training.
source: Participants in both groups learned CS–US contingencies during acquisition training, which was indicated by a CS-type main effect that consisted of enhanced responses to the CS+ as compared to the CS– in all dependent measurements, namely binary (yes/no), trial-wise US expectancy ratings (CS-type main effect in rmANOVAs: US expectancy F(1,44) = 203.9, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.823, mean difference: 0.578 ± 0.660/0.496 [95% CI], see Figure 1a), SCR (F(1,43) = 41.7, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.493, mean difference: 0.088 ± 0.115/0.061 [95% CI], see Figure 1b) and fear ratings: (F(1,44) = 116.0, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.725, mean difference: 0.361 ± 0.428/0.294 [95% CI]; see Figure 1c), see Supplementary file 1b for full statistics, means and CI.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and referenced figures.

claim: There was an interaction effect in US expectancy between CS-type, trial, and group-status during acquisition training.
source: Unexpectedly, we found an interaction effect in US expectancy between CS-type, trial, and group-status (i.e., subjects that were allocated to receive Placebo or L-DOPA on the next day: CS-type × trial × group F(2,88) = 3.3, p=0.044, ηp2 = 0.07).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Follow-up group comparisons of block-wise US expectancy did not support any differences in CS+ or CS− responses between groups during acquisition training.
source: However, follow-up group comparisons of block-wise US expectancy did not support any differences in CS+ or CS− responses (two-tailed independent post-hoc t-tests: p-values [FWE] >0.255, see Supplementary file 1c) or CS+/CS− discrimination between groups (p(FWE) > 0.65, CS discrimination was descriptively lower in the prospective Placebo vs. L-DOPA group, see Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no support for differences between groups in fear ratings or SCRs during acquisition training.
source: There was no support for differences between groups in fear ratings or SCRs (group main effect or interaction ps>0.1, see Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: On day 2, participants discriminated between CS+ and CS−, as indicated by a main effect of CS-type across all outcome measures.
source: On day 2, participants discriminated between CS+ and CS−, as indicated by a main effect of CS-type across all outcome measures (CS-type main effect in rmANOVAs: US expectancy: F(1,41)=22.3, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.353, mean difference: 0.183 ± 0.269/0.106 [95% CI], SCR: F(1,38)=23.9, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.386, mean difference: 0.065 ± 0.092/0.039 [95% CI], and fear ratings: F(1,41)=61.83, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.601, mean difference: 0.345 ± 0.434/0.256 [95% CI]; see Table Supplementary file 1d for full statistics).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Responses in all measures decreased over the time course of extinction training.
source: Responses in all measures decreased over the time course of extinction training (CS-type by block interaction, all ps<0.05, see Supplementary file 1d, see Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and referenced figure.

claim: Trial-wise US expectancy ratings indicated successful extinction learning of the CS–US association.
source: In particular, trial-wise US expectancy ratings indicated successful extinction learning of the CS–US association, i.e. differential CS responses in the first two blocks (CS+ > CS−, Block 1: p<0.001, Block 2 p=0.048), but not the last (Block 3: p=0.57, see Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The analyses of fear rating indicated only a weak support for an interaction between CS-type, block, and group during extinction training.
source: Importantly, the analyses of fear rating indicated only a weak support for an interaction between CS-type, block, and group (F(1,42)=3.884, p=0.059, ηp2 = 0.095).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Lower differential ratings of fear (CS+ − CS−) at the beginning of day two in the L-DOPA group when compared to placebo controls was not supported when correcting for multiple comparisons.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis, we found lower differential ratings of fear (CS+ − CS−) at the beginning of day two in the L-DOPA group when compared to placebo controls, but this difference was not supported when correcting for multiple comparisons (one-sided, post hoc independent t-test: L-DOPA < Placebo, t(41)=1.911, p(uncorr)=0.032, p(FWE-corr)=0.064, Cohen's d: –0.583, L-DOPA mean: 0.430 ± 0.523 [SD], Placebo mean: 0.682 ± 0.322 [SD], see Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no statistical support for reduced differential fear appraisal of the CSs in the L-DOPA group, as compared to the Placebo group during extinction training.
source: Hence, we found no statistical support for reduced differential fear appraisal of the CSs in the L-DOPA group, as compared to the Placebo group.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no statistical evidence that would support a difference between groups in US expectancy ratings or SCR during extinction training.
source: We further found no statistical evidence that would support a difference between groups in US expectancy ratings or SCR (see Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The fitted prediction error, associability, and learning rate did not differ between groups during extinction training.
source: The fitted prediction error (as a measure of expectancy violation), associability (as a measure of prediction error-guided surprise) and learning rate did not differ between groups (two-sided independent sample t-test for mean prediction error: t(40)=0.097, p(uncorr) = 0.923, p(FWE)>0.99; mean associability: t(40)=0.015, p=0.988, and mean learning rate: t(40)=0.179, p(uncorr)=0.859, p(FWE)>0.99; see Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling and statistical analysis.

claim: Participants discriminated between CSs in all outcome measures during retrieval test on day three.
source: Participants discriminated between CSs in all outcome measures (CS-type main effect in rmANOVAs: US expectancy: F(1,41)=23.21, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.361, mean difference: 0.253 ± 0.358/0.148 [95% CI], SCR: F(1,40) = 24.07, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.376, mean difference: 0.076 ± 0.108/0.045 [95% CI], and fear ratings: F(1,41) = 54.79, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.578, mean difference: 0.512 ± 0.652/0.372 [95% CI]; see Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: US expectancy ratings indicated a general reinstatement of CS+ and CS− responses when comparing the last three trials before and after the reinstatement USs.
source: US expectancy ratings further indicated a general reinstatement of CS+ and CS− responses, when comparing the last three trials before and after the reinstatement USs (see Supplementary file 1i), but not within a block-wise reinstatement analyses (see Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The SCR analyses of the three trials before and after reinstatement revealed a difference between groups in differential CS responses.
source: Importantly, the SCR analyses of the three trials before and after reinstatement revealed a difference between groups in differential CS responses (CS-type by group interaction F(1,40)=5.443, p=0.025, ηp2 = 0.120, see Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1i), indicating lower CS discrimination in the L-DOPA group when compared with the Placebo controls after the reinstatement procedure (one-sided, L-DOPA < Placebo post hoc t-test: t(40)=2.405, p(FWE-corrected)=0.020, Cohen's d = −0.741, L-DOPA mean: –0.006 ± 1.31 [SD], Placebo mean: 0.086 ± 0.116 [SD], see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and referenced figures.

claim: Post hoc comparisons of CS+ and CS− responses between groups did not support a difference between L-DOPA and Placebo after reinstatement.
source: Post hoc comparisons of CS+ and CS− responses between groups did not support a difference between L-DOPA and Placebo (p>0.19, see Supplementary file 1k).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Additional analyses that included two to five trials also revealed a difference between groups in differential SCRs after reinstatement.
source: Additional analyses that included two to five trials also revealed a difference between groups in differential SCRs (see Supplementary file 1l,m and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and referenced figures.

claim: L-DOPA administration during extinction training reduced differential threat responses after reinstatement.
source: While our a priory hypothesis was an effect of L-DOPA on the psychophysiological measurements at retrieval test on day 3, our analyses suggest that L-DOPA administration during extinction training reduced differential threat responses after reinstatement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Decreasing US expectancy during extinction training was accompanied by more pronounced signalling in the right vmPFC in the L-DOPA group as compared to the placebo group.
source: We found that decreasing US expectancy was accompanied by more pronounced signalling in the right vmPFC in the L-DOPA group as compared to the placebo group (see Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and referenced figure.

claim: Administration of L-DOPA augmented vmPFC activity during extinction learning, i.e., when participants decreased their US expectancy.
source: Thus, administration of L-DOPA augmented vmPFC activity during extinction learning, i.e., when participants decreased their US expectancy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: Higher individual vmPFC responses across groups that reflected decreasing US expectancy for the CS+ were associated with lower conditioned responses (SCR CS+ > CS−) during retrieval test 24 hr later.
source: Indeed, we found that higher vmPFC activation is associated with reduced differential SCR, which could indicate better individual extinction memory retention, 24 hr later (two-sided Pearson correlation: t(38) = –2.18, p-value=0.035, r = −0.3273302 [95% CI: –0.58 to 0.018, see Figure 3b]).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and referenced figure.

claim: There was no difference between groups detectable in SCRs during retrieval test.
source: Importantly, there was no difference between groups detectable in SCRs during retrieval test, which might have biased this correlation (Makin and Orban de Xivry, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and a citation about potential bias.

claim: There was support for a treatment effect of L-DOPA on SCRs during retrieval test, which was indirectly mediated by vmPFC activity during extinction learning.
source: Indeed, we found support for a treatment effect of L-DOPA on SCRs during retrieval test, which was indirectly mediated by vmPFC activity during extinction learning (average causal mediation effect: β = 0.0563, 95% confidence intervals = 0.007–0.12, p=0.038, quasi-Bayesian estimation of confidence intervals with 1000 iterations, N = 40, see Figure 3 for detailed statistics).
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis and referenced figure.

claim: L-DOPA strengthens vmPFC activation that accompanies decreasing expectation of the US (i.e., extinction learning), and this enhancement of vmPFC activity mediates reduced differential SCR 24 hr later (i.e., better extinction memory retrieval).
source: As such, L-DOPA strengthens vmPFC activation that accompanies decreasing expectation of the US (i.e., extinction learning), and this enhancement of vmPFC activity mediates reduced differential SCR 24 hr later (i.e., better extinction memory retrieval).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: L-DOPA has an effect on memory retrieval that is meditated by augmentation of vmPFC activity, which was specific for the individual time course of decreasing expectancy of the aversive outcome.
source: Our results thereby reveal an effect of L-DOPA on memory retrieval that is meditated by augmentation of vmPFC activity, which was specific for the individual time course of decreasing expectancy of the aversive outcome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Activation in the right nucleus accumbens in the Placebo group reflected the time course of the modelled prediction error term, but not in the L-DOPA group.
source: We found that activation in the right nucleus accumbens in the Placebo group reflected the time course of the modelled prediction error term, but not in the L-DOPA group (see Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and referenced figure.

claim: The nucleus accumbens in the Placebo group was responsive towards US omissions, only if an aversive outcome was still expected, which reflects the violation of the expected, yet omitted, value.
source: This suggests that the nucleus accumbens in the Placebo group was responsive towards US omissions, only if an aversive outcome was still expected, which reflects the violation of the expected, yet omitted, value.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI data.

claim: A cluster in the right nucleus accumbens reflected the expected value at the time-point of US omission.
source: This was supported by an exploratory follow-up analysis, revealing a cluster in the right nucleus accumbens that reflected the expected value at the time-point of US omission (MNI xyz: 9, 18, –4; Z = 3.04; pFWE-SVC=0.040).
evidence: This claim is supported by exploratory fMRI data analysis.

claim: Categorical responses at the time-point of US omission were higher in the L-DOPA group, compared to Placebo group.
source: We found that categorical responses at the time-point of US were higher in the L-DOPA group, compared to Placebo group (see Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and referenced figure.

claim: Responses in the Placebo group at the time-point of US omission were negative.
source: In fact, responses in the Placebo group were negative, which would be in line with our finding of expectancy violation coding in the nucleus accumbens: Expectancy violation would be characterised by positive responses in early trials of extinction training (when US expectancy is high) and decreases rapidly with decreasing US expectancy, which could lead to negative responses when averaging a whole time course.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data and theoretical interpretation.

claim: Enhancing dopaminergic transmission (i.e., in the L-DOPA group) seems to sustain responses to the omitted outcomes in the nucleus accumbens, irrespectively of expectancy of the US or value caching.
source: Enhancing dopaminergic transmission (i.e., in the L-DOPA group), in contrast, seems to sustain responses to the omitted outcomes in the nucleus accumbens, irrespectively of expectancy of the US or value caching.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI data.

claim: The results imply a dopaminergic modulation of expectancy violation in the nucleus accumbens when expected aversive outcomes are omitted during extinction training.
source: Hence, our results imply a dopaminergic modulation of expectancy violation in the nucleus accumbens when expected aversive outcomes are omitted during extinction training.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Within exploratory analyses there was no activity in the nucleus accumbens to CS+ presentations during extinction.
source: Note that within exploratory analyses that were suggested by the reviewers we found no activity in the nucleus accumbens to CS+ presentations during extinction (see Supplementary file 1n), which might suggest that the nucleus accumbens might rather be involved in processing of expectancy violation coding when expected USs are omitted.
evidence: This claim is supported by exploratory fMRI data analysis.

claim: During acquisition training, there was activity in the nucleus accumbens to presentations of the CS+ (as well as in the contrast CS+ > CS−) and the US.
source: During acquisition training, however, we found activity in the nucleus accumbens to presentations of the CS+ (as well as in the contrast CS+ > CS−) and the US (see Supplementary file 1n), which resembles salience encoding, as reported in a recent study in rodents (Cai et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and a citation to a rodent study.

claim: Administration of L-DOPA enhanced associability related neural signals in the amygdala at the time-point of US omission, when compared to Placebo.
source: We found that administration of L-DOPA enhanced associability related neural signals in the amygdala at the time-point of US omission, when compared to Placebo (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and referenced figure.

claim: Dopaminergic enhancement might enhance shifting of attention or surprise that is initiated by unexpected omission of the US during extinction training.
source: Our results suggest that dopaminergic enhancement might enhance shifting of attention or surprise that is initiated by unexpected omission of the US during extinction training.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the fMRI data.

claim: There was stronger connectivity between the nucleus accumbens and the amygdala in the L-DOPA group when compared to the Placebo group at the time-point of US omission.
source: In line with animal data, we found stronger connectivity between the nucleus accumbens and the amygdala in the L-DOPA group when compared to the Placebo group (contrast: L-DOPA > Placebo, see Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional connectivity analysis and referenced figure.

claim: Contrasting responses at the time-point of US omission that were specifically improved by dopaminergic enhancement in the L-DOPA group revealed strengthened connectivity between the nucleus accumbens and the substantia nigra/VTA (SN/VTA) complex.
source: Moreover, contrasting responses at the time-point of US omission that were specifically improved by dopaminergic enhancement in the L-DOPA group, without making any assumption about the Placebo group (contrast: L-DOPA ≥ Placebo), revealed strengthened connectivity between the nucleus accumbens and the substantia nigra/VTA (SN/VTA) complex, see Figure 5b.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional connectivity analysis and referenced figure.

claim: Coupling between the nucleus accumbens with the amygdala and the VTA was only observed to omitted USs during extinction learning.
source: Such coupling between the nucleus accumbens with the amygdala and the VTA was only observed to omitted USs during extinction learning, since additional control analyses did not conclusively support functional coupling between these regions during CS+ in extinction or acquisition training, as well as during US presentation in acquisition training (p(FEW) = 0.064; see table Supplementary file 1o).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional connectivity analysis and control analyses.

claim: The activity in the nucleus accumbens during the omitted US is functionally coupled with responses in the amygdala and the SN/VTA and this connectivity is enhanced by administration of L-DOPA.
source: Hence, the activity in the nucleus accumbens during the omitted US is functionally coupled with responses in the amygdala and the SN/VTA and this connectivity is enhanced by administration of L-DOPA.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the functional connectivity analysis.

claim: Dopaminergic processes are involved in threat extinction learning.
source: Our results provide evidence that dopaminergic processes are involved in threat extinction learning.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Dopaminergic enhancement during extinction learning augmented extinction memory at a later test, which was mediated by extinction-learning-specific vmPFC responses.
source: Dopaminergic enhancement during extinction learning augmented extinction memory at a later test, which was mediated by extinctio-learnin-specific vmPFC responses (i.e., reflecting decreasing US expectancy).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Decreased US expectancy in extinction learning was driven by dopaminergic activity within the nucleus accumbens that signalled the omission of expected aversive outcomes.
source: Decreased US expectancy in extinction learning was further driven by dopaminergic activity within the nucleus accumbens that signalled the omission of expected aversive outcomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Activity in the nucleus accumbens, when the US was omitted, was functionally coupled with the midbrain SN/VTA complex, as well as the amygdala.
source: This activity in the nucleus accumbens, when the US was omitted, was functionally coupled with the midbrain SN/VTA complex, as well as the amygdala.
evidence: This is a summary of the functional connectivity findings.

claim: The activity of the nucleus accumbens, but not the vmPFC, encoded absent threats (prediction error) during extinction learning.
source: Hence, our results suggest that the activity of the nucleus accumbens, but not the vmPFC, encoded absent threats (prediction error) during extinction learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Decreasing expectancy of threats in extinction learning was reflected by vmPFC activity, which was further enhanced by L-DOPA.
source: Decreasing expectancy of threats in extinction learning was reflected by vmPFC activity, which was further enhanced by L-DOPA.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The results corroborate findings from reinforcement learning in which outcome and prediction error signals were encoded in the striatum, whereas value was reflected by prefrontal regions.
source: These results corroborate findings from reinforcement learning in which outcome and prediction error signals were encoded in the striatum, whereas value was reflected by prefrontal regions (Jocham et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous research via citation.

claim: The main finding is that L-DOPA reduced retrieval of conditioned threat responses (SCR) by a mediation through enhanced vmPFC activity.
source: The main finding is that L-DOPA reduced retrieval of conditioned threat responses (SCR) by a mediation through enhanced vmPFC activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: Enhancement of dopaminergic transmission by the administration of L-DOPA during extinction learning enhanced individual neural signalling in the vmPFC that reflected the reduction of US expectation.
source: In detail, we found that enhancement of dopaminergic transmission by the administration of L-DOPA (as compared to Placebo) during extinction learning enhanced individual neural signalling in the vmPFC that reflected the reduction of US expectation (i.e., extinction learning).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental finding.

claim: Enhanced vmPFC responses were found to mediate the effect of L-DOPA on extinction memory retention, measured as reduced differential SCRs 24 hr later.
source: These enhanced vmPFC responses were found to mediate the effect of L-DOPA on extinction memory retention, measured as reduced differential SCRs 24 hr later.
evidence: This is a summary of the mediation analysis finding.

claim: The results align specifically with a previous finding of vmPFC activity pattern during extinction memory consolidation that mediates the effect of L-DOPA on extinction memory retention.
source: Our results align specifically with a previous finding of vmPFC activity pattern during extinction memory consolidation that mediates the effect of L-DOPA on extinction memory retention (Gerlicher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous research via citation.

claim: The results extend the finding on memory consolidation by providing a link between dopaminergic effects on vmPFC activity that are specific for individual extinction learning and augmentation of extinction memory.
source: Our results extend this finding on memory consolidation by providing a link between dopaminergic effects on vmPFC activity that are specific for individual extinction learning (i.e., decreasing US expectancy) and augmentation of extinction memory.
evidence: This is a conclusion about how the current findings extend previous research.

claim: L-DOPA might have the potential to improve (otherwise low) vmPFC activity during extinction learning.
source: L-DOPA might have the potential to improve (otherwise low, see parameter estimates in the Placebo group, Figure 3b) vmPFC activity during extinction learning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data.

claim: Rather than enhancing extinction learning per se, L-DOPA administration seems to augment vmPFC responses that accompany decreased US expectancy.
source: Hence, rather than enhancing extinction learning per se, L-DOPA administration seems to augment vmPFC responses that accompany decreased US expectancy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The findings would fit to previous results that link the benefit of neuropharmacological intervention in extinction learning to decreasing threat expectancies.
source: Our findings would fit to previous results that link the benefit of neuropharmacological intervention in extinction learning to decreasing threat expectancies (Sartori and Singewald, 2019; Gerlicher et al., 2019; Hofmann, 2014; Smits et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous research via citations.

claim: L-DOPA might have the potential for a psychopharmacological treatment that augments threat extinction learning instead of dampening overall threat responses, like classic anxiolytics.
source: Thereby, L-DOPA might have the potential for a psychopharmacological treatment that augments threat extinction learning instead of dampening overall threat responses, like classic anxiolytics.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about potential clinical applications.

claim: L-DOPA administration during extinction training reduced differential SCRs after reinstatement, which aligns with a finding of decreased SCRs after reinstatement by L-DOPA administration that followed extinction training in women diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder.
source: Additionally, we found that L-DOPA administration during extinction training reduced differential SCRs after reinstatement, which aligns with a finding of decreased SCRs after reinstatement by L-DOPA administration that followed extinction training in women diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (Cisler et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous clinical research via citation.

claim: Decrement of US expectancy in extinction training involves a dopaminergic coding of expectancy violation in form of a prediction error at the time-point of US omission.
source: A second set of our results implicate that decrement of US expectancy in extinction training involves a dopaminergic coding of expectancy violation in form of a prediction error at the time-point of US omission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Administration of L-DOPA enhanced general (categorical) activity during omitted US, which was paralleled by reduced prediction error signals that were found in the placebo group.
source: In detail, administration of L-DOPA enhanced general (categorical) activity during omitted US, which was paralleled by reduced prediction error signals that we found in the placebo group.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The enhanced general activity in the nucleus accumbens to omitted outcomes might results from enhanced activity in dopaminergic projections from midbrain, which would be in line with L-DOPA-induced dopamine release in the midbrain in humans at rest.
source: The enhanced general activity in the nucleus accumbens to omitted outcomes might results from enhanced activity in dopaminergic projections from midbrain, which would be in line with L-DOPA-induced dopamine release in the midbrain in humans at rest (Black et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: L-DOPA has been found to activate otherwise silent dopaminergic neurons in animals, which thereby might enhance activity in the nucleus accumbens in general.
source: L-DOPA has further been found to activate otherwise silent dopaminergic neurons in animals (Grace, 2008), which thereby might enhance activity in the nucleus accumbens in general.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to animal research.

claim: L-DOPA could have induced inhibitory signals (via dopamine D2-receptors) that limit phasic burst-firing and thereby reduce the pattern of prediction error encoding.
source: In parallel, L-DOPA could have induced inhibitory signals (via dopamine D2-receptors) that limit phasic burst-firing and thereby reduce the pattern of prediction error encoding (Beckstead et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: A shift in striatal activity by L-DOPA would fit to the observation of an opposite effect by blockade of dopamine D2 receptors (using haloperidol): reduced categorical activity during (rewarding) outcomes and enhanced prediction error signals.
source: Such a shift in striatal activity by L-DOPA would fit to the observation of an opposite effect by blockade of dopamine D2 receptors (using haloperidol [Wächtler et al., 2020]): reduced categorical activity during (rewarding) outcomes and enhanced prediction error signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current findings to previous research via citation.

claim: The findings align with a negative association between striatal dopamine synthesis capacity (measured by radiolabelled L-DOPA during positron emission tomography) and BOLD responses related to reward prediction errors.
source: Our findings furthermore align with a negative association between striatal dopamine synthesis capacity (measured by radiolabelled L-DOPA during positron emission tomography) and BOLD responses related to reward prediction errors (Schlagenhauf et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous research via citation.

claim: Higher dopamine synthesis capacity (indicated by uptake of L-DOPA in the striatum) was associated with lower prediction error related BOLD activity.
source: Hence, higher dopamine synthesis capacity (indicated by uptake of L-DOPA in the striatum) was associated with lower prediction error related BOLD activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from a cited study.

claim: The study was intentionally not designed to disentangle details of expectancy violation coding of omitted USs, but rather to provide a scenario of safety learning.
source: Our study was intentionally not designed to disentangle details of expectancy violation coding of omitted USs, but rather to provide a scenario of safety learning.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design and limitations.

claim: During extinction training, there was no involvement of the nucleus accumbens during presentations of the CS+, which is more in line with coding of expectancy violation rather than salience.
source: During extinction training, we found no involvement of the nucleus accumbens during presentations of the CS+, which is more in line with coding of expectancy violation rather than salience (see Supplementary file 1n).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from exploratory fMRI data analysis.

claim: During acquisition training, the nucleus accumbens was associated with salience encoding, since there was activation to presentations of the CS+ (and in the contrast CS+ > CS−), as well as the US.
source: During acquisition training, however, the nucleus accumbens was associated with salience encoding, since we found activation to presentations of the CS+ (and in the contrast CS+ > CS−), as well as the US (see Supplementary file 1n).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from exploratory fMRI data analysis.

claim: A recent study in rodents could disentangle encoding of salience and expectancy violation during extinction learning in lateral and medial part of the VTA, respectively.
source: A recent study in rodents could disentangle encoding of salience and expectancy violation during extinction learning in lateral and medial part of the VTA, respectively (Cai et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a rodent study.

claim: The study provides evidence for a role of the nucleus accumbens in processing of US omissions, which is in line with a function of the nucleus accumbens in rodents in particular during extinction learning.
source: While we cannot examine such fine-grained processes in the VTA with fMRI in humans, we nevertheless provide evidence for a role of the nucleus accumbens in processing of US omissions, which is in line with a function of the nucleus accumbens in rodents (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; Budygin et al., 2012) in particular during extinction learning (Correia et al., 2016; Holtzman-Assif et al., 2010; Rodriguez-Romaguera et al., 2012; Whittle et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous rodent research via citations.

claim: The results dovetail with two previous neuroimaging study reporting prediction error signals in the nucleus accumbens during extinction training.
source: Our results furthermore dovetail with two previous neuroimaging study reporting prediction error signals in the nucleus accumbens during extinction training (Thiele et al., 2021; Raczka et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous human neuroimaging research via citations.

claim: The results point to a dopaminergic modulation of surprise in the amygdala that is evoked by US omission, which fits well to previous reports of associability coding in the amygdala during threat learning.
source: Our results point moreover to a dopaminergic modulation of surprise in the amygdala that is evoked by US omission, which fits well to previous reports of associability coding in the amygdala during threat learning (Boll et al., 2013; Lindström et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous research via citations.

claim: Signals in nucleus accumbens at the time-point of US omission were functionally coupled with activation in the amygdala and the SN/VTA, which were enhanced by administration of the dopaminergic precursor L-DOPA.
source: We further show that signals in nucleus accumbens at the time-point of US omission were functionally coupled with activation in the amygdala and the SN/VTA, which were enhanced by administration of the dopaminergic precursor L-DOPA.
evidence: This is a summary of the functional connectivity findings.

claim: This finding mirrors findings in animals implying neurons in the VTA, as well as projections from the VTA to the nucleus accumbens, in the encoding of the omission of an expected US.
source: This finding mirrors findings in animals implying neurons in the VTA, as well as projections from the VTA to the nucleus accumbens, in the encoding of the omission of an expected US (Luo et al., 2018; Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to animal research via citations.

claim: The results would align with studies in animals that provided evidence for amygdala to nucleus accumbens projections that underlie extinction of threat responses.
source: Furthermore, our results would align with studies in animals that provided evidence for amygdala to nucleus accumbens projections that underlie extinction of threat responses (Correia et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to animal research via citation.

claim: Interaction between dopaminergic pathways and amygdala activity during threat extinction is in line with a study in rodents that revealed changes in inhibitory interneuron activity in the amygdala by dopaminergic projections from the VTA that enable suppression of freezing during early extinction.
source: Such interaction between dopaminergic pathways and amygdala activity during threat extinction is moreover in line with a study in rodents that revealed changes in inhibitory interneuron activity in the amygdala by dopaminergic projections from the VTA that enable suppression of freezing during early extinction (Aksoy-Aksel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to rodent research via citation.

claim: This pharmacological fMRI study in human volunteers is only suited to draw inferences on blood-oxygen-level-dependent signals as a function of L-DOPA administration.
source: This pharmacological fMRI study in human volunteers is only suited to draw inferences on blood-oxygen-level-dependent signals as a function of L-DOPA administration.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's limitations.

claim: The changes reported are only indirect markers of changes in dopaminergic neurotransmission.
source: Hence, the changes reported here are only indirect markers of changes in dopaminergic neurotransmission, which might suggest together with fine-grained studies in animals that dopaminergic neurotransmission is involved in extinction learning across species (Felsenberg et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's limitations and interpretation, supported by citations.

claim: Dopamine-specific markers in humans (e.g., using PET) might be suitable to unambiguously link changes in vmPFC and nucleus accumbens activity during extinction learning to dopaminergic neurotransmission.
source: Dopamine-specific markers in humans (e.g., using PET) might be suitable to unambiguously link changes in vmPFC and nucleus accumbens activity during extinction learning to dopaminergic neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on the study's limitations.

claim: The behavioural effects of pre-extinction administration of L-DOPA in this study were weaker when compared with studies that employed post-extinction administration.
source: The behavioural effects of pre-extinction administration of L-DOPA in our study were weaker when compared with studies that employed post-extinction administration (Gerlicher et al., 2018; Haaker et al., 2015; Haaker et al., 2013; Gerlicher et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous research via citations.

claim: There was no support in univariate analyses that L-DOPA administration decreased conditioned responding across all outcome measures during extinction learning and retrieval test.
source: We found no support in univariate analyses that L-DOPA administration decreased conditioned responding across all outcome measures that reflect different threat processing, such as US expectancy, psycho-physiological arousal (SCR), and affective (fear) ratings during extinction learning and retrieval test.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's findings.

claim: L-DOPA decreased differential SCRs during retrieval test by mediation via vmPFC activity during extinction learning, which converges with a previous finding.
source: Nevertheless, we found that L-DOPA decreased differential SCRs during retrieval test by mediation via vmPFC activity during extinction learning, which converges with a previous finding (Gerlicher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous research via citation.

claim: The current state of research might suggest that L-DOPA enhances vmPFC activity during or after extinction training, that could decrease threat responses, rather than blunting threat responses, per se.
source: Hence, the current state of research might suggest that L-DOPA enhances vmPFC activity during or after extinction training, that could decrease threat responses, rather than blunting threat responses, per se.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in the context of previous research.

claim: The current sample size was based on effect sizes that result from previous reports of post-extinction administration, and hence the sample size might have been too small to detect univariate differences between the L-DOPA and placebo group with sufficient power.
source: Our current sample size was based on effect sizes that result from previous reports of post-extinction administration (Gerlicher et al., 2018; Haaker et al., 2013), and hence our sample size might have been too small to detect univariate differences between the L-DOPA and placebo group with sufficient power.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's limitations, supported by citations.

claim: The results were derived from a population of healthy male volunteers and a role for L-DOPA in extinction learning within a representative sample, as well as populations with anxiety disorders have just been recently pioneered.
source: Our results were furthermore derived from a population of healthy male volunteers and a role for L-DOPA in extinction learning within a representative sample, as well as populations with anxiety disorders have just been recently pioneered (Cisler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's limitations and generalizability, supported by a citation.

claim: The results provide a neuropharmacological, dopaminergic mechanism for augmentation of neural substrates that underlie extinction learning in humans, which could provide a promising novel strategy to augment behavioural treatments of anxiety related disorders.
source: In sum, our results thereby provide a neuropharmacological, dopaminergic mechanism for agumentation of neural substrates that underlie extinction learning in humans (Gerlicher et al., 2019; Hofmann, 2014; Smits et al., 2013; Smits et al., 2013), which could provide a promising novel strategy to augment behavioural treatments of anxiety related disorders (Cisler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the clinical implications, supported by citations.

claim: Fifty healthy male subjects without self-reported psychiatric and neurological diseases, without current medication, or current use of illicit drugs were recruited in this study.
source: Fifty healthy male subjects without self-reported psychiatric and neurological diseases, without current medication (including no 'over the counter drugs' without prescription within the last 2 weeks), or current use of illicit drugs (urine toxicology) were recruited in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the study's participant recruitment criteria.

claim: The final sample in the analyses included 46 participants (L-DOPA N = 24, Placebo N = 22) between the age of 20 and 38 after exclusion of four subjects.
source: The final sample in the analyses included 46 participants (L-DOPA N = 24, Placebo N = 22) between the age of 20 and 38 (mean 27.07, SD = 4.18; L-DOPA mean = 27.29, SD = 4.102; Placebo mean = 26.82, SD = 4.35; two-sided unpaired t-test: t(44)=0.38, p>0.7) after exclusion of four subjects (positive drug urine test N = 1, incidental finding of a brain cyst N = 1, not following the instructions N = 1 and accidental press of the emergency bell N = 1).
evidence: This is a description of the study's final sample.

claim: The sample size of 40 participants (plus 10 drop-outs) was determined a priory in order to archive a power of 0.95 with an alpha level of 0.05 and assuming an effect size of eta2 = 0.08.
source: The sample size of 40 participants (plus 10 drop-outs) was determined a priory in order to archive a power of 0.95 with an alpha level of 0.05 and assuming an effect size of eta2 = 0.08 (previous effect of L-DOPA on extinction memory consolidation, G*Power 3.1.9.6, RRID:SCR_013726).
evidence: This is a description of the study's sample size calculation.

claim: Study medication included an oral administration of 150 mg L-DOPA (including 37.5 mg benserazide) in a double-blind and placebo-controlled protocol 60 min before extinction training.
source: Study medication included an oral administration of 150 mg L-DOPA (including 37.5 mg benserazide) in a double-blind and placebo-controlled protocol 60 min before extinction training.
evidence: This is a description of the study's medication protocol.

claim: The dose of 150 mg L-DOPA has been found effective in previous studies to enhance the consolidation of extinction memories in humans.
source: The dose of 150 mg has been found effective in previous studies to enhance the consolidation of extinction memories in humans (Gerlicher et al., 2018; Haaker et al., 2015; Haaker et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acquisition training (day 1) and extinction training (day 2) were conducted in the fMRI scanner, while retrieval test (day 3), including reinstatement, were employed within the psycho-physiological laboratory.
source: Using a three-day paradigm, acquisition training (day 1) and extinction training (day 2, approx. 24 hr after acquisition) were conducted in the fMRI scanner, while retrieval test (day 3, approx. 24 hr after extinction), including reinstatement, were employed within the psycho-physiological laboratory.
evidence: This is a description of the study's experimental procedure.

claim: Acquisition training took place in context A, whereas extinction training was employed in context B.
source: Acquisition training took place in context A, whereas extinction training was employed in context B.
evidence: This is a description of the study's experimental design.

claim: Retrieval test was conducted in a 50/50-mixture of context A and B in order to examine contextual generalisation, which also involves contextual renewal of conditioned threat responses.
source: Retrieval test (including reinstatement procedure) was conducted in a 50/50-mixture of context A and B in order to examine contextual generalisation (Andreatta et al., 2015), which also involves contextual renewal of conditioned threat responses (Vervliet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the study's experimental design, supported by citations.

claim: L-DOPA administration affected extinction training, while acquisition training, as well as retention and reinstatement tests were conducted drug free.
source: Twenty-four hours after acquisition training participants received L-DOPA (see Study medication) before the extinction learning session (the CS+ was no longer followed by an aversive outcome). L-DOPA administration thereby affected extinction training, while acquisition training, as well as retention and reinstatement tests were conducted drug free.
evidence: This is a description of the study's experimental design.
